beats.headline: Why does your business logic depend on your database?
beats.subline: Stop leaking JPA entities into your controllers.
beats.narration: Most Java apps are tightly coupled messes. When your JPA entity leaks into your controller, a database schema change breaks your JSON API. It is time to decouple.

beats.title: Ports and Adapters
beats.narration: Hexagonal architecture puts your domain in the center. Driving adapters call inbound ports, while your core calls outbound ports. The core never knows if it is talking to Postgres or a mock.

beats.title: Pure Domain Logic
beats.narration: Notice the core has zero Spring or JPA imports. It defines its own repository interface. You can test this service in milliseconds without booting a database container.

beats.title: Leaky vs. Clean Boundaries
beats.narration: Stop returning JPA entities from controllers. Map them to domain objects at the boundary. It prevents over-posting bugs and keeps your business rules safe from serialization side effects.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Enforcing architecture with ArchUnit →
beats.narration: That is the core. In Part 2, we use ArchUnit to ensure no one accidentally imports Spring into your domain package.

beats.headline: Does your architecture rot after every PR?
beats.subline: Stop relying on code reviews to catch dependency violations.
beats.narration: Diagrams are just suggestions. If you don't enforce your architecture in CI, someone will eventually import a JPA repository into your domain layer.

beats.title: ArchUnit Test
beats.narration: ArchUnit lets you write architectural rules as unit tests. If a developer imports Spring into the domain package, the build fails immediately. It is the ultimate guardrail.

beats.title: Onion Architecture
beats.narration: Onion architecture is just Hexagonal with layers. Dependencies only point inward. The domain knows nothing about the outside world. Keep it that way.

beats.title: CI Integration
beats.narration: When a rule breaks, you get a clear error message in your CI logs. No more guessing why a dependency graph is circular.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): CQRS for high-performance reads →
beats.narration: Automate your standards. In Part 3, we look at CQRS to separate your read and write models for massive performance gains.

beats.headline: Why are your read models so slow?
beats.subline: Stop using JPA aggregates for complex reporting screens.
beats.narration: JPA entities are great for writes, but terrible for complex reads. If you are doing 5-way joins just to show a dashboard, you need CQRS.

beats.title: CQRS Flow
beats.narration: CQRS separates commands from queries. You write to a normalized domain model and project that data into a flat, read-optimized table. No joins required.

beats.title: Read Projection
beats.narration: The projection is just a flat record. When an order is placed, we update this view. Queries become simple key-value lookups. It is lightning fast.

beats.title: Consistency Trade-offs
beats.narration: CQRS introduces eventual consistency. Your read model might be milliseconds behind the write model. Use optimistic UI updates to mask this delay.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
beats.narration: CQRS is powerful but adds complexity. In Part 4, we learn how to migrate a legacy monolith using the Strangler Fig pattern.

beats.headline: Stop the big-bang rewrite.
beats.subline: It never works. Use the Strangler Fig pattern instead.
beats.narration: Rewriting a monolith from scratch is a death sentence. Instead, strangle it. Extract one capability at a time until the monolith is gone.

beats.title: Strangler Fig Pattern
beats.narration: Place a gateway in front of your monolith. Route specific paths to your new service. Keep the rest on the monolith until you are ready to migrate.

beats.title: Anti-Corruption Layer
beats.narration: The Anti-Corruption Layer translates legacy garbage into clean domain objects. It keeps the new service's codebase pristine while it talks to the old system.

beats.title: Gateway Routing
beats.narration: Use a gateway like Spring Cloud Gateway to manage the transition. You can even route a small percentage of traffic to the new service as a canary.

beats.title: Part 4 Summary
beats.narration: Strangler Fig is the safest way to modernize. In Part 5, we discuss when a modular monolith is actually the best choice.

parts.partTitle: When to Use a Modular Monolith

beats.headline: Is your architecture over-engineered?
beats.subline: Sometimes, a simple modular monolith is all you need.
beats.narration: Hexagonal and CQRS are great, but they add serious overhead. If you are a small team, don't pay the tax until you have to.

beats.title: Modular Monolith
beats.narration: Organize by business capability, not technical layer. Use package-private classes to enforce boundaries. It is easier to maintain and faster to build.

beats.title: Pragmatism vs. Complexity
beats.narration: Start with a modular monolith. It gives you the seams you need to extract services later. Don't distribute your system until the load demands it.

beats.title: Final Checklist
beats.narration: Keep it simple. Use ArchUnit to keep your modules clean. Extract to microservices only when your team or load justifies the cost.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You have mastered architectural patterns. Checkout the roadmap for the full guide and lab exercises. Keep building clean systems.
